answer.summary:
Three editor classes define the DSB-free field. Cytosine base editors (Komor 2016) and adenine base editors (Gaudelli 2017) chemically convert one base pair into another within a small window using a deaminase fused to nickase Cas9; they are efficient but limited to transitions, cause bystander edits, and carry class-specific liabilities — CBEs produce guide-independent genome-wide SNVs (Zuo 2019) and both classes deaminate RNA transcriptome-wide (Grunewald 2019). Prime editing (Anzalone 2019) instead writes a template from an extended pegRNA via reverse transcriptase, covering all 12 substitutions plus small indels and, with twinPE, kilobase rearrangements; its cost is lower efficiency and a much larger cargo, which drove the PE4/PE5/PEmax mismatch-repair fixes (Chen 2021) and dedicated delivery engineering.

Delivery splits three ways. LNP-mRNA is transient, re-dosable in principle, and liver-tropic — it carried both macaque PCSK9 studies (Musunuru 2021, Rothgangl 2021) and all three in vivo human treatments. Dual AAV reaches brain, liver and heart but gives persistent editor expression (Davis 2023). Engineered VLPs deliver pre-formed ribonucleoprotein with no nucleic acid payload, minimizing exposure time; the platform was built for base editors (Banskota 2022), then extended to prime editors (An 2024) and refined for cargo loading (Cell 2025).

The evidence tiers are sharply unequal. Human clinical evidence exists only for base editing: ex vivo multiplexed CBE knockout in CAR7 T cells (Chiesa 2023, NEJM), an n-of-1 bespoke in vivo LNP-ABE therapy in an infant with CPS1 deficiency (Musunuru 2025, NEJM), and a 35-adult phase 1 dose-ascending LNP-ABE trial against PCSK9 (Vafai 2026, NEJM). Prime editing has no peer-reviewed human result in this set — its strongest evidence remains mouse (phenylketonuria correction, alternating hemiplegia rescue) and organoid work. Everything involving progeria, sickle cell HSPCs, Angptl3 and non-human primate PCSK9 is preclinical animal evidence, however convincing.
gaps: No peer-reviewed human clinical result for prime editing was found; the Prime Medicine chronic granulomatous disease program and similar trials have not surfaced as full papers in this search, so the clinical tier is base-editing-only.

BEAM-101 sickle cell data, the most advanced ex vivo base-editing program after CAR7, exist only as ASH/EHA conference abstracts rather than peer-reviewed papers, and were therefore excluded; a definitive publication may exist outside this search's reach.

OpenAlex was budget-exhausted and Semantic Scholar timed out on 7 of 8 search variants, so forward-citation coverage is incomplete and the citation edge list is a verified subset, not exhaustive; plausible edges (e.g. PE-eVLP citing the original eVLP paper) were omitted for lack of direct evidence.
No abstract was retrievable for Musunuru 2021 (Nature, PCSK9 in primates) from any index, so that entry carries an empty quote despite being a pivotal translational paper.

Long-term durability and immunogenicity evidence is thin: the macaque work reported anti-editor humoral responses blocking re-dosing, and the human trials report median follow-up of roughly 9 months or 7 weeks, so no multi-year human safety data exist.
Coverage of delivery to non-liver tissues in humans is absent; all in vivo human base editing to date is hepatic via LNP, and CNS, muscle and lung delivery remain preclinical.
Comparative head-to-head efficiency and off-target data between base editing and prime editing at matched therapeutic loci are sparse; the AHC paper is one of few that runs both.
Searches were English-language and index-driven; regulatory submissions, trial registry records and non-indexed clinical reports were not systematically covered.

answer.summary: Base editing and prime editing both avoid the double-strand breaks that drive indels, translocations and chromosomal loss in nuclease editing, but they trade off differently. Base editors (Komor 2016 for C•G-to-T•A; Gaudelli 2017 for A•T-to-G•C) are chemically simple, highly efficient, and now carry essentially all human in vivo evidence — but they are restricted to transition mutations within a narrow editing window and suffer bystander edits. Prime editing (Anzalone 2019) can install any substitution plus small insertions and deletions, and with twinPE extends to kilobase-scale rearrangements, but its larger, three-component architecture makes it harder to deliver and historically less efficient; PEmax/PE4-PE5 and epegRNAs closed much of that efficiency gap. Delivery sorts the evidence cleanly. LNPs deliver editor mRNA plus guide transiently to hepatocytes and are the only modality with published human in vivo results: VERVE-102 in 35 adults with heterozygous FH or premature CAD, and the bespoke k-abe therapy in a single infant with CPS1 deficiency. AAV (including dual-AAV splits) reaches brain, liver and heart in mice but requires high vector doses and provokes immune responses, and engineered virus-like particles — which deliver ribonucleoprotein DNA-free and should limit off-target exposure — remain entirely preclinical. Ex vivo editing of autologous or donor cells sidesteps delivery altogether and accounts for the rest of the human data: base-edited CAR7 T cells for T-ALL, risto-cel for sickle cell disease, and PM359, the only published prime-editing clinical result. Preclinical animal work (progeria, sickle cell, SMA, PKU, Chd3) establishes efficacy and mechanism; human work so far establishes only short-term feasibility and biomarker response in small, single-arm phase 1/2 cohorts.
gaps: No published human in vivo prime editing. The only clinical prime-editing data (PM359 for CGD, two patients) is ex vivo autologous HSPCs; in vivo prime editing remains at the dual-AAV mouse stage with acknowledged high-vector-dose and immunogenicity barriers.
Engineered virus-like particles have no human clinical data at all — the eVLP evidence base is entirely mouse and non-human primate.
All in vivo human base editing is liver-directed. GalNAc-LNP tropism confines the published clinical in vivo work to hepatocytes; extrahepatic in vivo delivery in humans is unpublished.

No comparative or randomized human evidence. Every human study listed is single-arm phase 1/2 with small n (1 to 35 patients) and short follow-up (months to ~1-2 years); no head-to-head base vs. prime vs. nuclease editing trial exists.

Long-term safety is unresolved. Off-target assays (CHANGE-seq-BE and similar) and RNA off-target analyses are laboratory measures, not clinical outcomes; no human data on oncogenic risk, durability beyond a few years, or germline consequences.

VERVE-101 (Heart-1), including the reported serious adverse event of transient ALT elevation with thrombocytopenia that halted enrollment, has no primary peer-reviewed publication I could verify — only a secondary review and conference reporting.
The risto-cel/BEAM-101 NEJM DOI (10.1056/nejmoa2504835) was resolved from an index listing rather than a scholarly abstract record, and I have no verbatim abstract text for it.

Tooling limits: OpenAlex was unavailable for the whole session and Semantic Scholar timed out on several queries, so seed reference lists could not be retrieved. Backward citation edges are therefore absent and the edge list below is incomplete — real citations certainly exist that I could not verify.

answer.summary:
Three design lineages anchor this field. Cytosine base editors (Komor 2016) and adenine base editors (Gaudelli 2017) fuse a deaminase to a Cas9 nickase to make single transition mutations within a narrow activity window — highly efficient but limited to 4 of 12 possible substitutions and prone to bystander edits. Prime editors (Anzalone 2019) use a reverse transcriptase and a pegRNA template to write arbitrary edits, trading breadth for lower initial efficiency; that gap has largely closed through PEmax/PE4-PE5 (Chen 2021), epegRNAs (Nelson 2022) and La-fusion PE7 (Yan 2024). Both avoid the indels, translocations and p53 activation of DSB editing.

Delivery splits by tissue. Ionizable LNPs carrying editor mRNA dominate the liver and are the only route with substantial human data; eVLPs deliver transient RNP to retina, brain and liver with lower off-target risk and no integration (Banskota 2022; An 2024); dual-AAV reaches postmitotic brain, liver and heart but persists as DNA (Davis 2024). LNP prime editing has only recently caught up with base editing, reaching ~49% bulk mouse liver editing in 2026.

Evidence tiers are sharply unequal. Preclinical animal work is broad and mature: progeria lifespan extension, sickle-cell HSC correction by both ABE and PE, PKU and metabolic liver correction, and two independent NHP PCSK9 studies. Human evidence is still narrow but is now genuinely clinical rather than anecdotal: ex vivo base-edited CAR7 T cells (3 children, 2023), ex vivo risto-cel for sickle cell disease (31 patients, 2026 — the largest dataset), in vivo LNP base editing of PCSK9 (35 adults, 2026 — the only randomized-scale in vivo result), a bespoke N-of-1 in vivo editor for CPS1 deficiency (2025), and first-in-human prime editing in 2 CGD patients (2026). Note that in the ex vivo cell therapies the dominant toxicity is busulfan conditioning, not the editor itself.
gaps: No published randomized controlled trial of any base or prime editor; all human data are single-arm phase 1/2, and the prime-editing clinical dataset is n=2.
Durability beyond ~1-2 years is unmeasured in humans; claims of 'one-and-done' editing rest on the permanence of the edit, not on observed long-term phenotype follow-up.
No in vivo (systemically delivered) prime editing has entered the clinic — all human prime editing to date is ex vivo HSC manipulation.
Extrahepatic in vivo delivery remains unsolved clinically: LNPs default to liver, and eVLP/AAV results for retina, brain, heart and HSCs are mouse- or NHP-only.

Guide-independent (Cas9-independent) deaminase off-target editing and transcriptome-wide RNA editing are characterized in cells and mouse embryos, but there is no sensitive human in vivo assay for them.
Immunogenicity of Cas9/deaminase/reverse-transcriptase proteins and anti-PEG or anti-capsid responses, which would block redosing, are poorly reported in the clinical papers.

Preclinical-to-human translation of editing efficiency is unquantified: no paper systematically relates mouse or NHP on-target percentages to the human liver editing levels inferred from VERVE-102 biomarkers.
Bespoke N-of-1 editing (baby KJ) has no established regulatory, manufacturing-reproducibility or cost framework, and its single-patient design cannot separate editing effect from supportive care.
Direct head-to-head comparisons of base vs prime editing for the same therapeutic target under identical delivery are essentially absent from the literature.

answer.summary:
Three design lineages anchor the field. Cytosine base editors (Komor 2016; Nishida 2016) and adenine base editors (Gaudelli 2017) install single transition mutations via a deaminase tethered to nicking Cas9 — simple, efficient, but limited to four of twelve substitutions and prone to bystander edits. Prime editing (Anzalone 2019) writes arbitrary edits from a pegRNA-encoded template, covering all substitutions plus small indels and, with twinPE (2022), kilobase rearrangements; the cost is lower efficiency and a larger, harder-to-deliver payload. Engineering follow-ups (ABE8e, PE4/PE5 MLH1dn, PE6) closed much of the efficiency gap.

Delivery splits along cargo size. Lipid nanoparticles carrying editor mRNA plus guide are the proven in vivo route for liver targets and underpin essentially all in vivo clinical data; engineered virus-like particles (Banskota 2022; An 2024; Geilenkeuser 2025) deliver pre-formed ribonucleoproteins transiently, giving markedly lower off-target editing and broader tropism, but remain preclinical. Dual-AAV split-intein constructs extend prime editing to non-dividing tissue such as brain and heart.

The preclinical/clinical boundary is sharp and worth stating plainly. Preclinical animal evidence is broad: progeria lifespan rescue, PCSK9 lowering in two independent macaque studies, PKU and alternating-hemiplegia correction, retinal and CNS editing. Human evidence is narrower. In vivo base editing has peer-reviewed patient data (VERVE-102 for hypercholesterolemia; the bespoke CPS1 infant case) and substantial unpublished company data (BEAM-302 in AATD). Ex vivo base editing has published outcomes in sickle cell disease and beta-thalassaemia. Prime editing's only published human data is ex vivo (PM359 in chronic granulomatous disease, two participants) — there is no in vivo prime editing clinical result as of this date, and eVLPs have not entered humans at all.
gaps: No in vivo prime editing clinical data exists yet; the modality's human evidence rests on two ex vivo CGD participants, and that trial reportedly paused recruitment for commercial rather than scientific reasons.
Engineered virus-like particles remain entirely preclinical despite strong off-target advantages — no published IND-enabling primate toxicology or first-in-human eVLP study was found.

Several high-profile in vivo base-editing results (BEAM-302 in AATD, VERVE-101 Heart-1) exist only as company press releases and conference abstracts, not peer-reviewed papers, so effect sizes and safety signals are not independently reviewed.
Human cohorts are very small (often 2-3 patients per dose level) with follow-up under ~12 months; durability, germline/off-target risk and delayed oncogenicity are unresolved.
Nearly all in vivo clinical work targets hepatocytes via LNP. Extrahepatic in vivo delivery (CNS, muscle, lung, HSCs in situ) has animal evidence only.

I did not verify whether the 2026 beta-thalassaemia and sickle-cell base-editing papers report in vivo or purely ex vivo protocols beyond the ex vivo autologous-HSC framing, nor their long-term engraftment data.
DOIs for the 2016-2024 foundational papers were drawn from model knowledge rather than re-fetched within the tool budget; spot-check before formal citation.
Head-to-head comparisons of base vs prime editing for the same therapeutic target, under matched delivery, are largely absent from the literature surveyed.

answer.summary:
I found 25 papers. The literature splits into two problems.

**1. Deskewing (one global rotation angle).** These methods estimate a single in-plane angle for a page whose text lines are straight, then rotate the image. The papers here cover two families:
- **Hough-based:** Hinds et al. 1990 (run-length encoding plus Hough), Singh et al. 2008, and Bezmaternykh & Nikolaev's Fast Hough Transform (2019).
- **Fourier-domain:** Fabrizio 2014, which a search result describes as ranked first in DISEC'13. I could not open the PDF, so I have no verified quote for it.

Projection-profile methods are the third classic family, but none was verified as a separate paper. Accuracy is measured on the ICDAR DISEC'13 contest with the AED, TOP80 and CE metrics; Bezmaternykh is the paper that documents this.

**2. Curved-page dewarping.** These methods have to recover a spatially varying non-rigid warp.
- **Early model-based work** fits a page model and inverts it: a general cylindrical surface (Meng et al., TPAMI 2012) or a fold prior (Common Fold, 2017).
- **Learned mappings, 2018 onward:** DocUNet started the line by regressing a dense 2D backward map. DewarpNet added a 3D-shape stage. Later work changed the mapping representation: patch flows (Li et al. 2019), transformer displacement fields (DocTr), control points (2022), TPS warps in Fourier space (FDRNet), and joint 3D/2D grids (UVDoc). Others add priors such as text lines (DocGeoNet, D2Dewarp), templates (Inv3D, DocMatcher) or axis alignment (AAD).
- **Recent work (late 2024 to 2026):** diffusion over coordinates (DvD), automatic real-data labelling by registration, book spreads (BookNet), and cascades. The cascade paper (2511.23150) applies a global affine/perspective correction before correcting curl. That is the most explicit link between the global and local problems.

**Benchmarks and evaluation.**
- **Datasets/contests:** CBDAR 2007 (OCR-based scoring), the DocUNet benchmark, DIR300 (from DocGeoNet), Inv3DReal, UVDoc and Book100.
- **New metrics:** DocMatcher's mnCER, the AAD metric, and the cascade paper's layout-aligned OCR metrics. All three argue that the usual MS-SSIM/LD/CER scores do not measure geometric quality reliably.

**Citation links.** The links listed come from Citation Lens reference-list edges. UVDoc's links were checked against its arXiv bibliography; the other edges come from index reference data. Almost all of them point back to DocUNet and DocTr. I found no verified citation links between the deskewing papers and the dewarping papers.
gaps: The ICDAR 2013 DISEC skew-estimation contest report (Papandreou et al.) and the classic Fourier (Postl 1986) and projection-profile (Baird 1987) skew papers could not be checked within the call budget, so they are not listed. Hull's 1998 skew survey is also missing.
The Fabrizio 2014 Fourier deskewing paper is included from a search result only. Its PDF would not parse, so its exact title and quote are unverified, and the quote is left empty.
The Hinds 1990 and Singh 2008 Hough papers had no abstract in the index, so their quotes are empty. The CBDAR 2007 contest quote is also empty because I could not verify the text.

answer.summary:
I found 25 papers. They split into two distinct problems.

**Global rotation (deskew).** This estimates one skew angle and undoes it with a rotation or affine transform. There are three classical families:
- **Projection profiles:** e.g. Li et al. 2007, which adds wavelets.
- **Hough transform:** covered in the Hull survey and Rehman & Saba 2011.
- **Fourier spectrum:** Peake & Tan 1997 is the classic. The modern refinement is Adaptive Radial Projection (Pham et al.), which works on ±44.9° skews and adds the DISE-2021 dataset.

DISEC 2013 is the standard deskew benchmark, using a ±15° range and a 0.1° tolerance. These methods are fast and need no training, but assume straight, parallel text lines, so they fail on curled pages.

**Curved-page dewarping.** This must estimate a dense non-rigid mapping. Learned methods began with DocUNet (2018), which regresses a forward map and also introduced a real-image benchmark. Later work went in several directions:
- **Explicit 3D shape:** DewarpNet adds 3D shape and the Doc3D dataset.
- **Transformers:** DocTr, the most-cited hub in this list.
- **Iterative refinement:** DocScanner.
- **Geometric priors:** DocGeoNet, grid regularization, UVDoc's 3D mesh plus 2D grid, and D2Dewarp use 3D, textline or grid constraints.
- **Annotation-light:** FDRNet works in the Fourier domain with thin-plate-spline warping.

Recent work (2025–26) adds diffusion over coordinate maps (DvD), progressive or time-aware formulations (TADoc), template matching (DocMatcher), two-page book spreads (BookNet), and cascaded pipelines. The cascaded method of Wang et al. 2025 runs the two problems in sequence: a global affine/perspective correction first, then curl and fold rectification.

**Evaluation.** This is a growing theme. PaperEdge showed that the standard MS-SSIM and LD metrics are flawed and proposed Aligned Distortion. Newer metrics are AAD, AD-M/AAD-M, mnCER, and layout-aligned OCR scores (AED/ACER). The DocUNet benchmark is now joined by new real benchmarks (AnyPhotoDoc6300, Book100). The pre-deep-learning reference is the CBDAR 2007 contest.

**Citation links.** Confirmed edges come from two sources:
- **Fourier skew paper's reference list, which I read:** it cites DISEC 2013, Peake & Tan and the Hull survey.
- **Citation-index edges and UVDoc's bibliography:** most recent dewarping papers cite DocTr; UVDoc also cites DocScanner and Deep Unrestricted Document Image Rectification.
gaps: The OpenAlex citation index hit its daily limit and Semantic Scholar timed out repeatedly. Forward and backward citation coverage is therefore partial: for example, DocUNet→DewarpNet and DewarpNet→DocTr links are almost certainly real but were not verified and are not listed.
I found no abstract text for DISEC 2013, Peake & Tan 1997, the Hull survey, Li et al. 2007 or Rehman & Saba 2011, so their quotes are empty.
The CBDAR 2007 dewarping contest PDF host was unreachable. Its details come from a web search summary, not the primary text, and its quote is empty.

Classic Hough-based deskew (Srihari & Govindaraju 1989), Postl's 1986 Fourier method and Fabrizio 2014's KNN-plus-Fourier method are known only from ARP's reference list. They have no resolved DOI or URL, so they are not included.
I did not find a peer-reviewed deep-learning deskew (global rotation regression or classification) paper; only low-impact journal items appeared.

I did not cover pre-deep-learning geometric dewarping (cylinder or shape-from-shading models, text-line snakes such as Bukhari et al. 2009), a dedicated dewarping survey (e.g., Wagdy et al. 2021), or the DIR300/DocAligner benchmarks, because the search budget ran out.

No paper here evaluates deskew and dewarping together or measures how each affects downstream OCR under one protocol. The 2025 metric papers each propose their own measure, and there is no consensus benchmark.

answer.summary:
I found 23 papers in two separate lines of work, with only light overlap.

**Global rotation (skew) correction**
- The classic methods are signal-processing estimators that look for one dominant angle:
  - Postl's projection/power-spectrum criterion (1986–88).
  - Hough-transform and projection-profile variants, surveyed by Hull (1998).
  - Fabrizio's kNN plus Fourier method (ICIP 2014), which won DISEC'13.
  - Adaptive Radial Projection on the DFT magnitude spectrum (ICIP 2022, posted to arXiv in 2026).
- They are evaluated on DISEC 2013 and DISE-2021, using angle error and how often the estimate falls within a tolerance.
- These methods are accurate, fast and need no training, but they assume a single rigid rotation of a flat page.

**Curved-page dewarping from a single image**
- Here a network learns a dense geometric mapping (a backward map or flow field, or a grid/mesh), mostly trained on synthetic data.
- Foundations: DocUNet (2D U-Net map plus the benchmark) and DewarpNet (3D shape, Doc3D dataset).
- Transformers and iterative flow: DocTr, DocScanner, DocTr++.
- Geometric priors: DocGeoNet/DIR300, RDGR's grid optimisation, Marior, UVDoc's coarse grids, D2Dewarp.
- FDRNet brings the Fourier view into dewarping.
- Work from 2024–2026:
  - A generative model that denoises coordinate maps (DvD, with the AnyPhotoDoc6300 benchmark).
  - Progressive, time-aware dewarping (TADoc).
  - Template-guided matching (DocMatcher).
  - Unified restoration models that include dewarping (DocRes).
  - Hybrid models with a parametric polynomial surface.
- Unrestricted methods such as DocTr++ correct rotation, perspective and curl together, so they partly absorb the global skew problem.

**Evaluation**
- Dewarping is mostly scored on DocUNet and DIR300 with MS-SSIM, LD and AD, plus OCR CER/ED.
- Recent papers dispute these metrics: a 2025 Pattern Recognition Letters metric paper, UVDoc's lighting-corrected MS-SSIM and line-straightness metric, TADoc's DLS and DocMatcher's mnCER.

**How the citation links were checked**
- From fetched reference lists: ARP, DvD and TADoc.
- From the search summaries:
  - UVDoc reports results on the DocUNet benchmark.
  - Fabrizio's method ranked first in the DISEC'13 contest.
  - The hybrid 2025 paper compares against DocGeoNet and DocTr++.
- From background knowledge, not checked in this session: DewarpNet citing DocUNet, and DocTr++ citing DocTr.
gaps: I hit the 8-call budget, so I couldn't open several abstracts. Most quotes are empty; only ARP, DvD and TADoc have checked verbatim snippets.

The links for DISEC 2013 (DOI 10.1109/ICDAR.2013.291) and DocGeoNet (arXiv 2210.08161) come from memory and were not checked. The Postl entry links to his patent instead of the 1986 ICPR paper, which I couldn't find a stable URL for.

Classic papers left out for lack of checked URLs: Baird's 'The skew angle of printed documents' (1987), Srihari & Govindaraju's Hough-transform paper (1989), Hull's 1998 skew survey, and Shafait & Breuel's CBDAR 2007 Document Image Dewarping Contest. The CBDAR contest is the main early dewarping evaluation paper.
Also left out: PaperEdge (SIGGRAPH 2022), DDCP control points (2021), LA-DocFlatten, DocReal, ForCenNet (ICCV 2025) and Inv3D.
I found no strong deep-learning global-skew paper with a public benchmark. Learned deskewing on DISEC/DISE-2021 looks under-studied next to Fourier/Hough baselines.
I didn't check citations between the skew and dewarping lines; they look largely disconnected.
The ARP paper's dates are inconsistent (ICIP 2022 paper, arXiv posting in March 2026). Check the venue before citing it.
There is no unified benchmark that tests rotation, perspective and curl together with agreed metrics, and the standard dewarping metrics (MS-SSIM/LD) are known to be unreliable.

answer.summary:
I found 19 papers. There are two separate problems here.

**Global rotation (deskew)** estimates one angle for the whole page and rotates it back. The classical family is projection profiles, the Hough transform and the Fourier spectrum. The Adaptive Radial Projection paper (Pham et al., ICIP 2022, posted to arXiv in 2026) is the modern representative: it reads the dominant angle off a radial projection of the 2D DFT magnitude. Its reference list traces back to Postl (1986), Peake & Tan (1997) and Hull's 1998 survey. Methods in this area are compared on DISEC 2013 and DISE-2021. Its own reference list includes no deep-learning skew methods.

**Single-image dewarping (curved pages)** needs a spatially varying mapping. Since 2018 this has been learned:
- **Dense displacement or backward maps:** DocUNet, DewarpNet (which adds 3D shape and the Doc3D dataset), DocTr and DocTr++ (transformers), DocScanner.
- **Geometry-constrained grids and lines:** DocGeoNet, RDGR, UVDoc, LA-DocFlatten, ForCenNet, D2Dewarp.
- **Bridging synthetic and real data:** PaperEdge, Marior.
- **Generative coordinate diffusion:** DvD.

FDRNet carries the Fourier idea into learned dewarping by working on high-frequency spectral components.

**Evaluation.** Results are reported on the DocUNet benchmark (MS-SSIM and Local Distortion), DIR300, WarpDoc, DocReal and the new AnyPhotoDoc6300, often alongside OCR edit distance and character error rate (ED/CER).

**Citation links.** The links from D2Dewarp, DvD and the Adaptive Radial Projection paper come from reading their reference lists. ForCenNet's links are inferred from the benchmarks it reports results on. The DewarpNet, DocTr and DocTr++ links come from my background knowledge of those papers and were not re-checked here.

**Verification.** Only five quotes were checked against the source text; the rest are left empty on purpose. The DOIs for DISEC 2013 and LA-DocFlatten were recalled from memory rather than confirmed, and SyntheticDoc was seen only in search results.
gaps: Missing classical primary sources (no DOI or URL confirmed, so left out): Postl 1986 (Fourier skew), Baird 1987 (projection profiles), Hull 1998 skew survey, and the CBDAR 2007 Document Image Dewarping Contest (Shafait & Breuel), which was the first dewarping benchmark.
No deep-learning deskew paper (CNN angle regression or classification) was found within the search budget. Learned global-rotation estimation is under-represented here.
Classical model-based curved-page methods (text-line fitting, cylindrical or developable-surface models, multi-view or 3D-scanner approaches) are not covered.
Missing because no URL was confirmed: DocMatcher (WACV 2025), DocReal (WACV 2024), Xie et al. displacement-flow and control-point methods, and the 2025 Mamba-based methods (DocMamba).
No recent survey covering both deep-learning dewarping and deskew was found. Wagdy et al. 2021 (IJIG) exists, but its content was not checked.
Concerns about metrics: MS-SSIM and LD on DocUNet are known to correlate poorly with OCR accuracy. Comparisons between AnyPhotoDoc6300 and the older benchmarks have not been independently reproduced.

papers.title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
papers.role: Foundational GPU I/O-aware exact attention kernel
papers.reason: Defines I/O-aware exact attention: tiling between HBM and SRAM gives linear memory, with an I/O-complexity analysis. All later kernels and distributed methods build on it.
papers.quote: We propose FlashAttention, an IO-aware exact attention algorithm that uses tiling to reduce the number of memory reads/writes between GPU high bandwidth memory (HBM) and GPU on-chip SRAM.

papers.title: Self-attention Does Not Need $O(n^2)$ Memory
papers.reason: Shows that exact attention can be computed in O(1)/O(log n) memory by chunking with a lazy softmax, before FlashAttention existed.
papers.quote: We present a very simple algorithm for attention that requires $O(1)$ memory with respect to sequence length and an extension to self-attention that requires $O(\log n)$ memory.

papers.title: Online normalizer calculation for softmax
papers.reason: The single-pass running max/normalizer trick that lets tiled exact attention avoid materializing the full score matrix.
papers.quote: In this paper we propose a way to compute classical Softmax with fewer memory accesses and hypothesize that this reduction in memory accesses should improve Softmax performance on actual hardware.

papers.title: FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning
papers.role: Parallelism / work partitioning within a GPU
papers.reason: Repartitions work across thread blocks and warps (including along the sequence dimension) to get closer to GEMM throughput.
papers.quote: We observe that the inefficiency is due to suboptimal work partitioning between different thread blocks and warps on the GPU, causing either low-occupancy or unnecessary shared memory reads/writes.

papers.title: FlashAttention-3: Fast and Accurate Attention with Asynchrony and Low-precision
papers.reason: Overlaps TMA data movement with Tensor Core compute through warp specialization and interleaves matmul with softmax. Only the FP16/BF16 exact path is in scope; the FP8 path is excluded.
papers.quote: exploiting asynchrony of the Tensor Cores and TMA to (1) overlap overall computation and data movement via warp-specialization and (2) interleave block-wise matmul and softmax operations

papers.title: FlashAttention-4: Algorithm and Kernel Pipelining Co-Design for Asymmetric Hardware Scaling
papers.reason: Redesigns the pipeline for Blackwell, where Tensor Core throughput outgrows shared memory and exponential units. Uses software-emulated exp and conditional rescaling, reaching 71% utilization on B200.
papers.quote: (2) software-emulated exponential and conditional softmax rescaling that reduces non-matmul operations, and (3) leveraging tensor memory and the 2-CTA MMA mode to reduce shared memory traffic

papers.role: Foundational distributed exact attention (ring / context parallelism)
papers.reason: Splits the sequence across devices and passes KV blocks around a ring, overlapping that communication with blockwise exact attention compute.

answer.summary:
I found 25 papers on memory-efficient exact attention, joined by 65 citation links from returned reference lists. The literature has three layers.

**1. Memory algorithms.** The online softmax normalizer (Milakov & Gimelshein, 2018), gradient checkpointing (Chen et al., 2016) and chunked lazy-softmax attention (Rabe & Staats, 2021) show that exact softmax attention never needs the full N×N matrix in memory. Blockwise Parallel Transformer extends the blockwise idea to fuse the feedforward network as well.

**2. I/O-aware GPU kernels.** FlashAttention turned those ideas into a tiled HBM↔SRAM kernel with an I/O-complexity bound. Each later version targets a different bottleneck:
- FlashAttention-2: work partitioning across thread blocks and warps, plus sequence-level parallelism.
- FlashAttention-3: Hopper asynchrony (TMA and warp specialization).
- FlashAttention-4 (2026): Blackwell's mismatch between fast Tensor Cores and slower exp/shared-memory units, via conditional rescaling and software exp.
- Lean Attention: decode-phase partitioning along the context length.
- FlexAttention and FlashMask: keep exactness and linear memory for arbitrary masks and score modifications through compiler generation or compact mask encodings.

**3. Distributed attention.** There are two main families plus newer hybrids:
- Ring/P2P (Ring Self-Attention, then Ring Attention): rotates KV blocks around devices, overlapped with compute. Striped Attention and DistFlashAttn fix causal load imbalance; BurstAttention also optimizes per-device memory access.
- All-to-all head parallelism (DeepSpeed Ulysses): simple, but limited by the number of heads.
- Hybrids: USP and LoongTrain combine both in 2D. Mesh-Attention (2025) tiles the Q-KV matrix in 2D for lower communication. Tree Attention uses a tree reduction for decoding. Context Parallelism applies ring-style attention to million-token inference prefill. FPDT and Untied Ulysses (2026) attack the remaining activation memory with pipelining, offloading and head-wise chunking.

Overall, single-GPU work has moved from memory to throughput on each new hardware generation. Distributed work has moved from simply making long contexts fit to balancing communication, load and activation memory.

**Exclusions (deliberately not listed):**
- Approximate or sparse attention: Reformer, Performer, Linformer, BigBird, MInference, SpargeAttention, and linear attention or its sequence parallelism (LASP, ZeCO).
- Low-precision variants: SageAttention 1/3, INT-FlashAttention, ThriftAttention, and FlashAttention-3's FP8 path.
- Serving and KV-cache policies: PagedAttention/vLLM, KIVI, KVQuant, MQA/GQA head sharing.

They change the computed result or target cache management rather than exact-attention memory or I/O.

answer.summary:
I found 25 papers on memory-efficient exact attention.

**Foundational memory algorithms.** Three ideas recur throughout the field:
- Online softmax with a running max and normalizer (Milakov & Gimelshein, 2018).
- Recomputation, i.e. trading compute for memory (Chen et al., 2016).
- Chunked exact attention in sublinear memory (Rabe & Staats, 2021).

**GPU I/O-aware kernels.** FlashAttention (2022) combined online softmax and recomputation into an IO-aware tiled kernel, with an IO-complexity analysis and lower bound.
- FlashAttention-2 changed the work partitioning across thread blocks and warps to raise utilization.
- FlashAttention-3 (Hopper) and FlashAttention-4 (Blackwell, 2026) co-design the kernel with each new GPU, using asynchrony, warp specialization and softmax rescaling.
- FlexAttention and FlashMask make the fused exact kernel programmable and support complex masks at linear memory.
- Lean Attention and DASH address work partitioning in decode and backward-pass scheduling.

**Distributed attention.** Two families dominate:
- Ring/context parallelism: Li et al.'s Ring Self-Attention, Blockwise Parallel Transformer leading to Ring Attention, DISTFLASHATTN, Striped Attention, BurstAttention and Meta's pass-KV/pass-Q inference variants. These circulate KV (or Q) blocks and overlap that communication with blockwise compute. Their main problems are load imbalance under causal masks and communication that grows with sequence length.
- All-to-all head partitioning: DeepSpeed Ulysses. It uses less communication, but its parallelism is capped by the number of attention heads.

Hybrid and 2D designs combine the two: USP, LoongTrain, ATTENTION2D and Mesh-Attention. Tree Attention uses a topology-aware tree reduction for decoding. Untied Ulysses adds head-wise chunking to cut activation memory.

**Trends since 2024.** Recent work focuses on hardware-specific kernel co-design, communication-optimal 2D partitioning, and memory-aware context parallelism.

**Citation evidence.** Most citing→cited links come from Citation Lens reference-list edges. A few come from the citing paper's abstract naming the earlier work outright: FlashAttention-2 naming FlashAttention, FlashAttention-4 naming FlashAttention-3, USP, Mesh-Attention and Untied Ulysses naming Ulysses and Ring Attention, and FlexAttention and FlashMask naming FlashAttention.

papers.quote: We propose FlashAttention-2, with better work partitioning to address these issues.

papers.title: FlashAttention-3: Fast and Accurate Attention with Asynchrony and Low-precision

papers.role: Memory algorithm bridging the single-device and distributed settings

papers.title: Sequence Parallelism: Long Sequence Training from System Perspective

papers.reason: Applies stream-K style partitioning to exact decode attention so SMs stay balanced at long context lengths, extending the Flash-Decoding idea.

answer.summary:
I found 19 papers that fit the request. They fall into three layers.

**1. Algorithms.** The online softmax normalizer (Milakov & Gimelshein, 2018) and chunked lazy-softmax attention (Rabe & Staats, 2021) show that exact attention can be computed blockwise without ever materializing the n×n matrix.

**2. Single-GPU kernels.** FlashAttention (2022) turned this into an I/O-aware fused kernel. Each later version targets the bottleneck of its hardware generation:
- FlashAttention-2 changed how work is split across thread blocks and warps.
- FlashAttention-3 (Hopper) added asynchrony and warp specialization.
- FlashAttention-4 (Blackwell, March 2026) treats the exponential units and shared-memory bandwidth, not matmul, as the limit, and redesigns the pipeline around them.

Two related lines of work:
- FlexAttention (MLSys 2025) generalizes the kernel via a compiler, trading a small amount of peak speed for programmability.
- Lean Attention and the Flash-Decoding idea (a blog post, not listed) split decoding work along the KV sequence to keep the GPU busy.

**3. Distributed attention.** There are two main styles:
- **Ring / point-to-point.** Li et al.'s sequence parallelism, then Blockwise Parallel Transformer → Ring Attention. Ring Attention overlaps passing KV blocks between devices with computation. Its causal-mask load imbalance is addressed by Striped Attention, DistFlashAttn and RingX (SC 2025).
- **Head all-to-all.** DeepSpeed Ulysses. Its communication volume stays constant, but the parallel degree cannot exceed the number of attention heads.

Hybrids (USP, LoongTrain) combine the two in a 2D layout. For inference, two 2024 papers adapt the approach:
- Tree Attention replaces the ring with a topology-aware tree reduction for decoding.
- Meta's Context Parallelism uses pass-KV and pass-Q ring variants to reach a 1M-token prefill.

**Excluded by design** (these appear only here, not in the paper list):
- Approximate or sparse attention, such as linear or low-rank attention and MTraining's dynamic sparse context parallelism.
- Low-precision variants, such as FP8 or INT8 attention. FlashAttention-3 is listed for its exact BF16 kernel only.
- KV-cache serving policies such as PagedAttention, eviction and compression, and FlashInfer-style serving engines.

**Citation links.** These come from the abstracts and well-known reference lists of these papers. I did not open each paper's bibliography to check, apart from what the searches showed.
gaps: I could not confirm the MagiAttention arXiv paper (heterogeneous-mask context parallelism, built on FlashAttention-3), so it is not in the list. I also left out other 2025–26 context-parallelism papers I could not check, such as FCP (arXiv 2605.08524).
Some quotes are blank. With the 8-call budget I could not read the abstracts of Sequence Parallelism, DistFlashAttn, Striped Attention, USP, LoongTrain and Lean Attention.
Most citation links rest on known reference lists, not on a page-by-page check. The RingX → Ring Attention link rests on its abstract comparing against 'conventional ring attention'.
Flash-Decoding exists only as a blog post, so it is not in the list. Kernel DSL papers such as ThunderKittens and FlashMask (exact masked attention) were also left out for budget reasons.
Backward-pass memory/IO analysis and lower bounds beyond FlashAttention's IO-complexity result are not covered.
Non-NVIDIA hardware (AMD, TPU, Ascend) exact-attention kernels and distributed attention over non-uniform interconnects remain thinly covered.

Few papers co-design kernels and distributed attention end-to-end, for example combining FlashAttention-4-style pipelining with ring or all-to-all overlap. Head-to-head benchmarks are emerging, e.g. the Long-Context Attention Benchmark (arXiv 2510.17896), but are not yet standard.

papers.reason: Introduced tiling plus backward-pass recomputation between HBM and SRAM. Attention memory becomes linear in sequence length and the result stays exact.
papers.quote: We propose FlashAttention, an IO-aware exact attention algorithm that uses tiling to reduce the number of memory reads/writes between GPU high bandwidth memory (HBM) and GPU on-chip SRAM.

answer.summary:
Memory-efficient exact attention starts from two algorithms. Online softmax (Milakov & Gimelshein 2018) normalizes in one pass with a running max and rescaling. Rabe & Staats (2021) chunked exact attention to O(1) or O(log n) memory. Recomputation (Chen et al. 2016) adds the idea of recomputing values instead of storing them.

**GPU I/O-aware kernels.** FlashAttention (2022) turned these ideas into a fused, tiled, I/O-aware GPU kernel. Each later version adapts the work partitioning to the hardware:
- FlashAttention-2: parallelizes over the sequence and splits work between warps.
- FlashAttention-3: Hopper asynchrony, warp specialization and TMA.
- FlashAttention-4 (2026): Blackwell, where tensor cores outpace shared-memory bandwidth and exp units. It uses async MMA, emulated exp, conditional rescaling and 2-CTA MMA in the backward pass.

The most recent kernel work (2024–2026) is about programmability and mask flexibility rather than new algorithms. FlexAttention generates kernels with a compiler, ThunderKittens offers tile DSL primitives, and FlashMask and MagiAttention's FFA kernel handle rich masks. All of them keep exact semantics.

**Distributed attention.** Two families exist:
- **Ring P2P:** Sequence Parallelism (Li et al.), then BPT, Ring Attention, Striped Attention and DistFlashAttn. These pass KV blocks between devices and overlap communication with compute. Their weak point is causal load imbalance.
- **All-to-all head re-sharding:** DeepSpeed-Ulysses. It is simple and fast within a node, but the degree of parallelism is capped by the number of heads.

USP and LoongTrain combine both in 2D. Tree Attention replaces the ring with a logsumexp tree reduction for decoding. Context Parallelism for inference (pass-KV/pass-Q) and TokenRing change the communication pattern. MagiAttention generalizes load balancing to arbitrary masks. LongCA-bench (2025) benchmarks kernels and CP schemes in one framework.

Overall, the kernels reduce HBM traffic within a device, and the distributed methods trade communication volume (ring) against head-parallel limits (all-to-all). Recent work mostly addresses load balancing and irregular masks.

**Notes on the evidence.**
- FA4's arXiv metadata and the LongCA-bench citations were checked on the papers' pages. The other citation edges come from well-known reference lists and were not each checked in this session.
- Several quotes were left empty rather than reconstructed from memory without verification.
gaps: Exclusions (by request): approximate attention (sparse, linear, low-rank, e.g., Performer, Reformer, sparse-attention CP like MTraining) is left out of the list. So are low-precision variants (the FP8 path of FlashAttention-3, SageAttention-style INT8/FP4 kernels) and serving KV-cache policies (PagedAttention/vLLM, KV eviction or compression, FlashInfer-style serving engines, Flash-Decoding/FlashDecoding++ heuristics).
MagiAttention has no standalone arXiv paper that I could find. Its description comes from the MAGI-1 report and project documentation, and its performance claims are self-reported.

Most citation edges, except the LongCA-bench ones checked on its page, were not confirmed against each paper's reference list in this session. Edges among the 2024–2026 distributed papers (e.g., TokenRing->USP, USP->Striped/DistFlashAttn) were left out for lack of verification.
The tool budget did not allow covering non-NVIDIA hardware: AMD/ROCm and TPU kernels, and Ring Attention's JAX/TPU results beyond the original paper.

The 2025–2026 distributed-attention literature looked thin in search. Possible additions include RingX (SC'25, ACM DOI 10.1145/3712285.3759859), HSAP (arXiv 2606.30460) and other hierarchical/topology-aware CP papers, but these were not checked.
Formal I/O-complexity lower bounds for attention beyond FlashAttention's own analysis (e.g., later theory papers on attention I/O complexity) were not checked or included.

papers.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
papers.reason: Introduces frozen-weight fine-tuning with trainable low-rank update matrices added to Transformer layers; the starting point for this whole lineage.
papers.quote: LoRA, which freezes the pre-trained model weights and injects trainable rank decomposition matrices into each layer of the Transformer architecture, greatly reducing the number of trainable parameters

papers.title: Intrinsic Dimensionality Explains the Effectiveness of Language Model Fine-Tuning
papers.reason: Shows that fine-tuning has a low intrinsic dimension. This is the direct motivation for LoRA's low-rank hypothesis, and LoRA cites it.
papers.quote: there exists a low dimension reparameterization that is as effective for fine-tuning as the full parameter space.

papers.title: Measuring the Intrinsic Dimension of Objective Landscapes
papers.reason: Introduced training in random low-dimensional subspaces to measure intrinsic dimension. Aghajanyan et al. built their analysis on this idea.
papers.quote: Many problems have smaller intrinsic dimensions than one might suspect

papers.title: Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning for NLP
papers.reason: Adapter modules on frozen backbones started parameter-efficient transfer learning. LoRA cites them as the main baseline.
papers.quote: On GLUE, we attain within 0.4% of the performance of full fine-tuning, adding only 3.6% parameters per task.

papers.title: Prefix-Tuning: Optimizing Continuous Prompts for Generation
papers.reason: A frozen-LM alternative that learns continuous prefixes. It is a standard comparison point for LoRA and its follow-ups.
papers.quote: by learning only 0.1\% of the parameters, prefix-tuning obtains comparable performance in the full data setting, outperforms fine-tuning in low-data settings

papers.title: The Power of Scale for Parameter-Efficient Prompt Tuning
papers.reason: Showed that soft prompt tuning approaches full fine-tuning as models grow. A prompt-based counterpart to low-rank adaptation.
papers.quote: as models exceed billions of parameters, our method "closes the gap" and matches the strong performance of model tuning (where all model weights are tuned).

papers.title: Towards a Unified View of Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning
papers.reason: Treats adapters, prefix tuning and LoRA as changes to hidden states, which places LoRA inside the wider PEFT design space.
papers.quote: we re-frame them as modifications to specific hidden states in pre-trained models, and define a set of design dimensions along which different methods vary

papers.title: QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs
papers.reason: The most widely used memory-efficient variant: it trains LoRA adapters on top of a frozen 4-bit (NF4) backbone, so a 65B model can be fine-tuned on one GPU.
papers.quote: QLoRA backpropagates gradients through a frozen, 4-bit quantized pretrained language model into Low Rank Adapters~(LoRA).

papers.title: LoftQ: LoRA-Fine-Tuning-Aware Quantization for Large Language Models
papers.reason: Quantizes the model and picks the LoRA initialization together, which reduces the quantization gap left by QLoRA.
papers.quote: a novel quantization framework that simultaneously quantizes an LLM and finds a proper low-rank initialization for LoRA fine-tuning.

papers.title: AdaLoRA: Adaptive Budget Allocation for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
papers.reason: Writes LoRA updates in SVD form and prunes singular values to spread the rank budget across weight matrices.
papers.quote: AdaLoRA parameterizes the incremental updates in the form of singular value decomposition.

papers.title: DoRA: Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation
papers.reason: Splits weights into magnitude and direction and applies LoRA only to the direction. This narrows the gap to full fine-tuning at no extra inference cost.
papers.quote: DoRA decomposes the pre-trained weight into two components, magnitude and direction, for fine-tuning, specifically employing LoRA for directional updates

papers.title: PiSSA: Principal Singular Values and Singular Vectors Adaptation of Large Language Models
papers.reason: Initializes the adapters from the principal singular components of W and freezes the residual, which speeds up convergence.
papers.quote: PiSSA shares the same architecture as LoRA, but initializes the adaptor matrices $A$ and $B$ with the principal components of the original matrix $W$

papers.title: LoRA+: Efficient Low Rank Adaptation of Large Models
papers.reason: Shows that LoRA's shared learning rate for A and B is suboptimal at large width and fixes it with a ratio between the two rates.
papers.quote: this suboptimality of LoRA can be corrected simply by setting different learning rates for the LoRA adapter matrices A and B with a well-chosen ratio.

papers.title: A Rank Stabilization Scaling Factor for Fine-Tuning with LoRA
papers.reason: Proves that the adapter scale should be 1/sqrt(r) rather than 1/r, so higher ranks become useful (rsLoRA).
papers.quote: we study the impact of the scaling factor on the learning process and prove that LoRA adapters should be divided by a factor of the square root of the rank.

papers.title: VeRA: Vector-based Random Matrix Adaptation
papers.reason: Shares one pair of frozen random low-rank matrices across all layers and trains only scaling vectors.
papers.quote: It achieves this by using a single pair of low-rank matrices shared across all layers and learning small scaling vectors instead.

papers.title: GaLore: Memory-Efficient LLM Training by Gradient Low-Rank Projection
papers.reason: Moves the low-rank idea from the weights to the gradients, allowing full-parameter learning with LoRA-like memory use.
papers.quote: we propose Gradient Low-Rank Projection (GaLore), a training strategy that allows full-parameter learning but is more memory-efficient than common low-rank adaptation methods such as LoRA.

papers.title: LoRA-GA: Low-Rank Adaptation with Gradient Approximation
papers.reason: Initializes LoRA so its first-step gradients match those of full fine-tuning, which fixes slow convergence.
papers.quote: aligns the gradients of low-rank matrix product with those of full fine-tuning at the first

papers.title: LoRA-Pro: Are Low-Rank Adapters Properly Optimized?
papers.reason: Shows that LoRA optimization equals full fine-tuning with a low-rank gradient, then adjusts gradients to better approximate full fine-tuning.
papers.quote: using LoRA for optimization is mathematically equivalent to full fine-tuning using a low-rank gradient for parameter updates.

papers.title: LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less
papers.reason: A large comparison on code and math: LoRA trails full fine-tuning on the target task but forgets less, and full fine-tuning learns much higher-rank updates.
papers.quote: full finetuning learns perturbations with a rank that is 10-100X greater than typical LoRA configurations

papers.title: LoRA vs Full Fine-tuning: An Illusion of Equivalence
papers.role: Recent analysis (2024-10, LoRA vs full FT)
papers.reason: A spectral analysis that finds 'intruder dimensions' in LoRA-trained weights. These distinguish LoRA from full fine-tuning even when accuracy matches.
papers.quote: weight matrices trained with LoRA have new, high-ranking singular vectors, which we call \emph{intruder dimensions}, while those trained with full fine-tuning do not.

papers.title: Initialization using Update Approximation is a Silver Bullet for Extremely Efficient Low-Rank Fine-Tuning
papers.reason: LoRA-SB approximates full fine-tuning inside the low-rank subspace using the LoRA-XS architecture and an optimal initialization.
papers.quote: We propose a method, LoRA Silver Bullet or LoRA-SB, that approximates full fine-tuning within low-rank subspaces using a carefully designed initialization strategy.

papers.title: LoRA-One: One-Step Full Gradient Could Suffice for Fine-Tuning Large Language Models, Provably and Efficiently
papers.reason: Proves that LoRA adapters align with singular subspaces of the one-step full fine-tuning gradient, and uses this for initialization.
papers.quote: We rigorously prove that, under gradient descent, LoRA adapters align with specific singular subspaces of the one-step full fine-tuning gradient.

papers.title: Parameter Efficient Fine-tuning via Explained Variance Adaptation
papers.role: Recent variant (2024-10, data-driven init + adaptive rank)
papers.reason: EVA initializes LoRA from activation-variance directions, which provably maximizes the expected gradient signal, and allocates ranks adaptively.
papers.quote: we introduce Explained Variance Adaptation (EVA), an initialization scheme that uses the directions capturing the most activation variance, provably maximizing the expected gradient signal

papers.title: ScaLoRA: Optimally Scaled Low-Rank Adaptation for Efficient High-Rank Fine-Tuning
papers.reason: Picks a loss-optimal low-rank matrix at each update so that accumulated updates reach high rank and approximate full fine-tuning.
papers.quote: Specifically, the per update optimal low-rank matrix is identified to minimize the loss function and closely approximate full fine-tuning.

papers.title: Low-Rank Adaptation Redux for Large Models
papers.reason: A 2026 re-examination of LoRA as the standard PEFT method for foundation models; useful as an up-to-date synthesis.
papers.quote: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has emerged as the de facto standard for parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of foundation models

answer.summary:
The lineage has three stages.

**Foundations.** Two older strands feed into LoRA:
- **Intrinsic dimension:** Li et al. (2018) trained networks in random low-dimensional subspaces, and Aghajanyan et al. (2020) showed that language-model fine-tuning has a low intrinsic dimension.
- **Parameter-efficient transfer:** Houlsby-style adapters, prefix-tuning and prompt tuning all train a small number of parameters on a frozen backbone.

LoRA (2021) joins these strands. Its reference list shows it citing both the adapter paper and Aghajanyan et al. It models the weight update as BA with low rank r, which can be merged into the weights so inference costs nothing extra. He et al.'s unified view then placed LoRA in the wider design space of PEFT methods.

**Follow-ups split into four families:**
1. **Memory-efficient:** QLoRA (4-bit NF4 backbone plus LoRA adapters) and LoftQ (quantization chosen jointly with the LoRA initialization). GaLore moves the low-rank idea from the weights to the gradients, so all parameters can still be trained with LoRA-like memory use.
2. **Reparameterized or structured updates:** AdaLoRA (SVD form with an adaptive rank budget), DoRA (separate magnitude and direction), PiSSA (adapters started from the principal singular components) and VeRA (shared random matrices with trainable scaling vectors).
3. **Optimization and scaling fixes:** LoRA+ (different learning rates for A and B), rsLoRA (1/sqrt(r) scaling), and LoRA-GA and LoRA-Pro (bringing LoRA's gradients closer to full fine-tuning's).
4. **Analyses of LoRA versus full fine-tuning:**
   - Biderman et al. (2024): LoRA learns less on the target domain but forgets less, and full fine-tuning learns updates of 10–100× higher rank.
   - Shuttleworth et al. (Oct 2024): LoRA creates "intruder dimensions" that full fine-tuning does not, even when accuracy matches.

**Recent work (2024-10 to 2026) mostly tries to close the remaining gap to full fine-tuning through initialization and theory.** LoRA-SB, LoRA-One and EVA start from gradient- or activation-derived subspaces, and ScaLoRA builds high-rank updates one optimal step at a time. "Low-Rank Adaptation Redux" (2026) is an up-to-date synthesis.

**Overall:** reparameterizations such as DoRA and PiSSA change what is learned; initialization and optimizer fixes (LoRA+, rsLoRA, LoRA-GA, LoRA-Pro, LoRA-One) change how it is learned; memory methods (QLoRA, GaLore) change what it costs. answer.summary:
LoRA's lineage has three stages.

**Foundations.** Li et al. (2018) and Aghajanyan et al. (2020) showed that training and fine-tuning can succeed inside very low-dimensional subspaces. LoRA's introduction names both papers as its inspiration. It turned their random-subspace idea into trainable low-rank updates (ΔW = BA) that can be merged into the weights. Adapters (Houlsby et al.), prefix tuning and prompt tuning were the parameter-efficient baselines LoRA set out to beat; it says adapters add inference latency and prompt-based methods use up sequence length.

**Follow-ups, 2022–2024.** They fall into five groups:
- **Memory efficiency:** QLoRA (4-bit frozen base model plus LoRA); GaLore (low-rank gradients and optimizer state with full-rank weights).
- **Rank allocation:** AdaLoRA, DyLoRA.
- **Parameter sharing:** VeRA (shared random matrices plus trained scaling vectors).
- **Scaling and optimization fixes:** rsLoRA, LoRA+, LoRA-Pro.
- **Reparameterization and initialization:** DoRA (magnitude/direction split), PiSSA (principal-SVD initialization), LoRA-GA (gradient-aligned initialization), MoRA (high-rank square update).

**LoRA vs full fine-tuning.** The analysis work centers on this comparison:
- *LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less* (2024): LoRA underperforms full fine-tuning on code and math but forgets less, and full fine-tuning learns updates of 10–100x higher rank.
- *Illusion of Equivalence* (Oct 2024): LoRA-trained weights contain 'intruder dimensions' in their spectra, and LoRA's forgetting is concentrated there.
- *LoRA Without Regret* (Thinking Machines, Sep 2025, blog post): LoRA matches full fine-tuning for RL even at small rank, and for small-to-medium SFT, provided it is applied to all layers (especially MLPs), uses about 10x the learning rate, and the dataset doesn't exceed adapter capacity.
- **2025 variants** mostly try to close the remaining gap: LoRA-SB and LoFT imitate full fine-tuning's update or optimizer dynamics, and RandLoRA gets full-rank updates from random bases.

**Overall trend.** Early variants reduced parameters and memory. Recent work tries to reproduce full fine-tuning's dynamics and spectral structure.

**Citation links.** All links come from Semantic Scholar reference lists, except two kinds:
- LoRA's links to the intrinsic-dimension papers, adapters, prefix tuning and prompt tuning come from LoRA's introduction text or its reference list.
- The blog post's outgoing links come from one page fetch whose summary listed which papers it names. That step was done by a summarizing model, so treat these links as moderate-confidence.
gaps: OpenAlex hit its daily limit during the run, so forward-citation coverage relied on Semantic Scholar alone (capped at 1,000 citing papers per seed). Influential follow-ups may be missing.

Coverage of 2026 papers is thin. The one targeted search for 2025–26 LoRA-vs-full-fine-tuning analyses mostly returned off-topic results, and one Semantic Scholar query timed out. No peer-reviewed 2026 comparison study was confirmed.

The AdaLoRA abstract was unavailable from the index, so its quote is left empty. VeRA, AdaLoRA, rsLoRA and GaLore have only some of their incoming links verified; for example, no evidence was found that VeRA cites LoRA, although it almost certainly does.

'LoRA Without Regret' is a non-peer-reviewed technical blog post. Its quote and outgoing citations come from one page fetch processed by a summarizing model and should be checked against the post itself.
Some LoRA references were not checked, including Rebuffi et al. 2017 (residual adapters) and Hambardzumyan et al. (WARP).

Not covered: other notable variants (LoRA-FA, LoftQ, LQ-LoRA, Tied-LoRA, LoRA-XS, MiLoRA, OLoRA), mixture-of-LoRA-experts methods, and theoretical analyses (e.g. 'The Expressive Power of Low-Rank Adaptation', arXiv 2310.17513). All appeared in the citation graph but were left out to keep the list focused.

answer.summary:
LoRA brings together two earlier lines of work.

- **Parameter-efficient transfer:** Houlsby-style adapters and prefix-tuning showed that a frozen backbone can be adapted with a small number of added parameters.
- **Intrinsic dimensionality:** Li et al. (2018) and Aghajanyan et al. (2020) showed that fine-tuning happens in a very low-dimensional subspace.

LoRA turned that observation into a mergeable low-rank update ΔW=BA that adds no inference latency. Follow-ups fall into a few groups:

- **Memory efficiency:** QLoRA (4-bit frozen base) and LoftQ. GaLore moves the low-rank idea from the weights to the gradients and optimizer states.
- **Reparameterization and initialization:** DoRA (magnitude/direction split), PiSSA and MiLoRA (SVD-based initialization), LoRA-GA (gradient-aligned initialization) and VeRA (shared random bases with trained scaling vectors).
- **Rank and optimization fixes:** AdaLoRA (adaptive rank), rsLoRA (√r scaling), LoRA+ (separate learning rates for A and B) and LoRA-Pro (gradient correction).

Analyses comparing LoRA with full fine-tuning have shifted from "LoRA matches full fine-tuning" (the original paper) to a more qualified picture:

- **Learns less, forgets less:** LoRA lags in the target domain but retains more of the base model's abilities (Biderman et al. 2024).
- **Different solutions:** LoRA's structurally different solutions show up as intruder dimensions (Shuttleworth et al., NeurIPS 2025).
- **Rank plateaus:** adding rank stops closing the gap (RandLoRA, ICLR 2025).
- **When LoRA can win:** theory says LoRA can beat full fine-tuning when the task shift is effectively low-rank (Zindari et al. 2026).

The 2026 evaluation papers (Learning Rate Matters; Beware of the Batch Size) find that many reported gains of variants over vanilla LoRA shrink to about 1–2% once learning rate and batch size are tuned. Meanwhile gradient-based methods such as LoRA-GA, LoRA-Pro and GDLoRA (Sep 2026) keep targeting the remaining gap to full fine-tuning.

answer.summary:
LoRA (2021) brought together two earlier lines of work. The first is intrinsic-dimensionality research: Li et al. 2018 trained networks in random subspaces, and Aghajanyan et al. 2020 showed that fine-tuning pretrained LMs has a very low intrinsic dimension. The second is parameter-efficient transfer: Houlsby adapters, prefix-tuning and prompt tuning. From there the follow-ups split into four branches.

1. **Memory-efficient methods.** QLoRA adds a 4-bit quantized base model. GaLore moves the low-rank structure from the weights to the gradients and optimizer states, which allows full-parameter learning.
2. **Reparameterized or structural variants.** DoRA splits weights into magnitude and direction. AdaLoRA allocates rank adaptively. VeRA uses shared random matrices plus trained vectors. MoRA uses square high-rank updates. GraLoRA (2025) uses block-wise adapters.
3. **Initialization and optimization fixes.** PiSSA, LoRA-GA and IniLoRA initialize from SVD components, gradients or early full-FT differences. LoRA+, rsLoRA and Stable-LoRA correct learning-rate and scaling dynamics.
4. **Comparisons with full fine-tuning.** Biderman et al. 2024 found that LoRA learns less but forgets less. Shuttleworth et al. 2024 found 'intruder dimensions' that make LoRA and full FT spectrally different even at equal accuracy. A 2026 theory paper identifies when LoRA can beat full FT: when the downstream shift is effectively low-rank. MoLF (2026) mixes the two per parameter.

A consistent 2026 finding cuts against the variant literature: once learning rate (Lee et al.) and batch size (Beware of the Batch Size) are tuned per method, vanilla LoRA roughly matches DoRA, PiSSA and similar methods. Many reported gains appear to come from hyperparameter bias.

**How the citation links were checked.** Links from GraLoRA, Learning Rate Matters and the 2026 theory paper were confirmed against their reference lists. MiLoRA is cited in Learning Rate Matters but is not in my paper list, so no edge was added for it. The remaining edges were not fetched this session. They rest on well-established knowledge of each paper's content: LoRA's related work and baselines, the VeRA comparison in DoRA, and QPiSSA building on QLoRA in PiSSA.
gaps: My research budget (8 tool calls) did not allow checking every citation edge against reference lists. Edges from the older follow-ups (QLoRA, DoRA, AdaLoRA, GaLore, PiSSA, VeRA, LoRA+, rsLoRA, MoRA, LoRA-GA, Biderman, Illusion) back to LoRA are near-certain but were not fetched this session.
11 of the 25 papers have an empty quote because I could not verify abstract text in this session.
'LoRA Without Regret' (Thinking Machines, Schulman et al., 2025) is an influential blog-style analysis of LoRA vs full FT, including in RL, but it is not an arXiv paper, so I left it out.

Several 2025 LoRA theory papers were not covered, for example on convergence and on the claim that one full gradient step suffices (LoRA-One). Also not covered: MiLoRA, ReLoRA, LongLoRA, mixture-of-LoRA and multi-adapter serving (S-LoRA, Punica), and BitFit as a concurrent baseline.
I did not confirm whether the 2026 variants (Stable-LoRA, MoLF, IniLoRA) cite LoRA, DoRA or PiSSA, so no edges were added for them.
I did not find independent evidence on which 2025-26 variants hold up once baselines are tuned. The evidence on tuned comparisons is still limited to a few papers.
